Getting started with DietView

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

Stomach contents are rarely identified to a single depth. A shrimp may be named to species, a fish fragment only to “Teleostei”, and a bolus of digested tissue to nothing at all. DietView keeps every one of those records, attaches a taxonomic lineage to it, and lets you look at the diet at all ranks at once, with the material that could not be identified below a given rank kept in view.

This vignette runs one complete analysis on the example table that ships with the package. The table is invented: 24 prey records from 11 stomachs of three predators. That is enough to show every step and far too little to say anything about what these fish eat, so read the numbers below as a demonstration of the mechanics only. The vignette “A known diet” uses a larger simulated survey to show what keeping unidentified records changes.

library(DietView)

1. One row per prey record 

dat <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
head(dat[, c("predator_species_common_name", "stomach_id", "verified_name",
             "prey_weight", "digestion_level_id")])
#>   predator_species_common_name stomach_id      verified_name prey_weight
#> 1                 Atlantic cod      GM001  Pandalus borealis        12.3
#> 2                 Atlantic cod      GM001   Ammodytes dubius         5.1
#> 3                 Atlantic cod      GM001           Decapoda         2.0
#> 4                 Atlantic cod      GM002 Themisto libellula         0.8
#> 5                 Atlantic cod      GM002          Teleostei         8.0
#> 6                 Atlantic cod      GM003  Pandalus borealis         9.0
#>   digestion_level_id
#> 1                  2
#> 2                  3
#> 3                  4
#> 4                  2
#> 5                  4
#> 6                  1

Each row is one prey taxon found in one stomach, with its wet weight in grams and a digestion score from 1 (fresh) to 5 (unrecognizable). There are no taxonomy columns. DietView adds them in step 3.

2. Say which column is which 

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator   = "predator_species_common_name",
  stomach    = "stomach_id",
  prey_id    = "aphia_id",        # WoRMS AphiaID, used first when present
  prey_name  = "verified_name",   # scientific name, used when there is no ID
  weight     = "prey_weight",
  digestion  = "digestion_level_id",
  covariates = c("period", "region")
)
dv_validate(dat, spec)
#> 24 records from 11 stomachs of 3 predator(s); 1 stomach(s) hold a single record; 0 record(s) lack a weight.

The specification changes nothing in your table. It records which column plays which role, so the original data never have to be renamed, and it can be saved next to your results. dv_validate() stops if a declared column is missing or a weight is negative, warns about records with no prey key, weights that are not numbers and stomach IDs shared between predators, and ends with a one-line description of the sample.

3. Attach the taxonomy

The example ships with a lineage table: one row per prey name, one column per rank.

lin <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example_lineage.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
lin[lin$verified_name %in% c("Pandalus borealis", "Decapoda", "unidentified material"), ]
#>           verified_name  kingdom     phylum        class    order     family
#> 1     Pandalus borealis Animalia Arthropoda Malacostraca Decapoda Pandalidae
#> 3              Decapoda Animalia Arthropoda Malacostraca Decapoda       <NA>
#> 7 unidentified material     <NA>       <NA>         <NA>     <NA>       <NA>
#>      genus           species
#> 1 Pandalus Pandalus borealis
#> 3     <NA>              <NA>
#> 7     <NA>              <NA>

Look at how incomplete identifications are stored. Decapoda has an order but no family, genus or species, and unidentified material has nothing. Those empty cells are not errors. They record where identification stopped, and DietView keeps them.

prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lin, verbose = FALSE)
prep
#> <dietview_prep>
#>   records   : 24 
#>   stomachs  : 11 
#>   predators : 3 
#>   ranks     : kingdom > phylum > class > order > family > genus > species 
#>   covariates: period, region 
#>   source    : table

With your own data you would normally query the World Register of Marine Species once, read the matching report, and save the result as a lineage table for every later run:

prep_online <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")   # needs 'worrms' and an internet connection
dv_taxonomy_report(prep_online)                            # fuzzy and unresolved matches

Saving the lineage fixes the taxonomic snapshot your figures were made from. Note the date and the worrms version alongside it, because WoRMS changes.

4. Count the diet at every rank 

tree <- dv_build_tree(prep$data, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
cls  <- dv_rank_table(tree, "Class")
cls
#>           label value_item value_occ   pct_occ value_w        pct_w
#> 10 Malacostraca          7        11 45.833333 39.7600 51.504725584
#> 9      Copepoda          2         4 16.666667  0.0048  0.006217874
#> 11    Teleostei          3         3 12.500000 35.1000 45.468205936
#> 8    Polychaeta          1         2  8.333333  0.7030  0.910659509
#> 12     Bivalvia          1         2  8.333333  0.0290  0.037566324
#> 13           NA          1         2  8.333333  1.6000  2.072624772

value_occ is the number of prey records assigned to each class, and pct_occ its share of all records. value_w and pct_w do the same for weight. Every record appears once in every ring of the tree: under the taxon it was identified to at that rank or, if identification stopped earlier, in an NA node below the last rank it reached. The denominator is therefore the same at every rank, here all 24 records or 77.2 g, and each ring adds up to 100%.

The two currencies tell different stories. Malacostraca make up 45.8% of the records, and fish (Teleostei) only 12.5%, yet the fish account for 45.5% of the weight. Records tell you how often a kind of prey turns up; weight tells you how much it contributes. Report both, or say which one you chose.

A note on names: pct_occ is a share of records. It is not the frequency of occurrence (%FO) of the diet literature, which is the proportion of stomachs containing a prey and does not add up across prey. dv_fo_table() gives %FO:

fo <- dv_fo_table(prep, rank = "class")
fo[fo$taxon == "Malacostraca", ]
#>    rank        taxon n_stomachs n_total pct_fo
#> 1 class Malacostraca          7      11  63.64

Malacostraca account for 11 of the 24 records but turn up in 7 of the 11 stomachs, because several stomachs hold more than one malacostracan.

5. How much was identified? 

na_share <- sapply(prep$ranks, function(r) {
  tb <- dv_rank_table(tree, tools::toTitleCase(r))
  round(sum(tb$pct_occ[tb$label == "NA"]), 1)
})
na_share
#> kingdom  phylum   class   order  family   genus species 
#>     8.3     8.3     8.3    37.5    58.3    62.5    62.5

In this table 37.5% of the records are unidentified at order and 62.5% at species. A statement about species would rest on fewer than half of the records, and digestion does not remove prey at random, so that half is not a random sample. This is why DietView keeps the unidentified nodes: they show how far a fine-rank statement can be trusted.

6. Draw it 

dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", title = "All predators, share of prey records")

The figure is interactive, so it is drawn on the package website rather than in this installed vignette. The center is the kingdom ring and each ring outward is one rank finer. White wedges with gray edges are records not identified at that rank. Hovering shows the count and the share. When you compare panels, build one palette from the pooled data and pass it to every panel (see the article on covariates).

7. Digestion 

dg <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep)
dg[, c("digestion", "finest_rank", "n_records", "p_records")]
#>    digestion finest_rank n_records p_records
#> 1          1     Species         2 100.00000
#> 2          2       Class         3  33.33333
#> 3          2       Order         2  22.22222
#> 4          2     Species         4  44.44444
#> 5          3       Class         2  28.57143
#> 6          3       Order         2  28.57143
#> 7          3      Family         1  14.28571
#> 8          3     Species         2  28.57143
#> 9          4       Class         2  50.00000
#> 10         4       Order         1  25.00000
#> 11         4     Species         1  25.00000
#> 12         5  Unresolved         2 100.00000

For each digestion score, the table gives the share of records whose deepest identified rank is species, genus, and so on, or none at all. With 24 records, two of them at score 1 and two at score 5, it cannot show a trend; it only shows the layout. The digestion vignette explains how to read it on real data.

8. Before you report

  • State the currency of every percentage: records, numbers or weight.
  • Report the unidentified share at the rank you discuss (step 5).
  • Give the taxonomic source and its date, or archive the lineage table.
  • If you aggregated rare prey (dv_aggregate_threshold()), give the threshold.
  • Archive the specification and the code with the figures.
  • Cite the package and the version you used. citation("DietView") gives the reference, “DietView: An R package for interactive, hierarchical visualization of predator stomach-content data”.

9. Share it 

dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "diet.html"),
              strata = c("period", "region"))
run_dietview(prep)   # interactive exploration, needs 'shiny'

The HTML file opens in any browser and needs neither R nor an internet connection. It is a snapshot: it shows the data as they were when you built it.
